I've been waiting for a laser cutter I ordered last year and was hoping to do some work making weird holiday decorations, but it's one of those Kickstarter things and has been delayed until December. So I've been looking into starting an amateur telebase space program.

You see, last year the ESA introduced their moonbase concept based on a design by Foster+Partners. I wondered why, after all ths time, the ESA hasn't started some project to demonstrate this concept because, in reality, it's not so high-tech and sophisticated. It's construction concept is a derivative of a method called 'mound form shell' construction that was used by German military engineers in WWII. It's also been used in more recent times to build an interesting arboretum in Japan called Grin Grin Park that I often use as an example of how real space settlements are likely to look. (the one major difference being that there wouldn't be dome windows but heliostat and artificial lighting arrays.) So it takes no very elaborate technology to do this--which is the whole point to having simple telerobots do it.

Trying to fight depression lately (thanks to ongoing legal problems with work) I've been watching a lot of videos about the hobby of RC construction models. I find them calming, like watching an aquarium. They're more well known in Europe than in the US, where racing models dominates, but these models have become very sophisticated in recent years and are designed not only for visual realism but functional realism. They are fully functioning, often featuring miniature hydraulics power systems and first-person video systems. At their largest usual scale or 1/8th they're about the same size as those robots proposed in the Foster design and, of course, there are a number of tractors and excavators of similar form. All over Europe they have these meets and shows where they make miniature villages and construction sites to put these models through their paces moving shipments arounds, assembling buildings and structures, and making roads and landscape features, all cooperatively.

So it occurred to me that you could make perfectly practical telerobots starting with these models and their components. We now have drop-in WiFi replacements for conventional RC transmitters so we can put these models on-line and control them over the Internet. Thus it's possible to demonstrate this moonbase construction, even full-scale, using a bunch of these RC models or home-brew robots derived from them and do it as an internet community project, like the community model train layouts. This is significant since it was at one particular model train layout that the concept of 'hacking' was invented and which was the origin of many of our modern principles of computing and digital control. The Tech Model Railway Club at MIT.

I've been floating this notion around the Internet to see what sort of interest I can scare up. Perhaps there are some commercial sponsors who might help--since there is sometimes help from construction equipment and truck companies for these RC model exhibitions. I've got a robot I've been planning to build for a while and these models might be an affordable source of parts. Not quite sure where it would be located or what specific materials can be used with such robots--conventional concrete might be a bit too messy to work with. So I'm giving this some study this summer.

Dude. Honestly. You might really be on to something right there. I don't own any commercial business but I can tell you that you have a great idea. Also the whole moon base thing is really cool. I hope that it goes well for you this summer, and I hope that your legal troubles subside too.
